scenes.name: one turn, thirty milliseconds
scenes.visual: Dark canvas, one continuous shot. It opens on the generate-loop panel rebuilt exactly as ch01_s05 left it: a large rounded panel (x 200-1720, y 300-800) titled 'the generate loop'. Inside, left to right: a blue box 'text so far' holding ch01's pills in two rows, 'the quick brown fox jumps' over 'over the lazy dog'; an arrow; a coral box 'run the whole model' with the small 40-tile weight grid inside it (coral means a weight being read); an arrow; a blue box 'one new token'. A return arrow runs from 'one new token' down and back along the panel's bottom edge to 'text so far', labelled 'append, go round again'. New here: a stopwatch icon at (1600, 215), above the panel's top right, showing '?'. From b2 the panel scales to 55% and parks in the top band (centre 960, 250), still turning slowly at 40% opacity; the centre band (y 560) becomes a one-second ruler and the bottom band (y 700-880) a compact copy of ch00's chat window. In b4 everything fades back except the stopwatch reading, and ch00's spec-sheet card returns. Colour: tokens blue, the expensive model step coral, the spec sheet's compute line amber and memory line coral, text white and grey. The idea: one turn is one token is about 30 ms; laid end to end that is a stream faster than reading; and the number can be derived.

beats.say: One turn of that loop takes about thirty milliseconds, three hundredths of a second.
beats.show: The panel is on screen from the first frame; the stopwatch with its '?' fades in above its top right. On 'One turn', copies of the nine pills flow into the coral box and its tiles light top to bottom; the '?' becomes '0 ms' and the stopwatch starts. On 'thirty milliseconds', a new blue pill '.' pops into 'one new token' and the stopwatch stops at '30 ms'; a small grey tag under it reads 'slowed down', since the turn took about two seconds of screen time. On 'three hundredths', a grey line writes under the reading: '= 0.03 s'.

beats.say: That is about thirty-three tokens a second, so words stream out at least as fast as you read. Exactly the target.
beats.show: The '.' pill rides the return arrow and appends to the row. The panel scales to 55% and slides into the top band at 40% opacity, still turning slowly; the stopwatch keeps reading '30 ms'. In the centre band a ruler draws from x 260 to x 1660, '0' to '1 s', ticks every 0.1 s, so 1,400 px is one second. Blue pills drop onto it one every 42 px, which is every 30 ms, slowed 4× so the second fills in about four seconds; grey tag under the ruler's left end: 'slowed 4×'. A counter above the ruler's right end (1560, 480) runs 0 to 33 as the last pill lands, label 'tokens in 1 s'. In the bottom band ch00's chat window returns with 'Why is the sky blue?', its answer streaming in step with the ruler, each token landing as a blue pill and relaxing into text. On 'as fast as you read', a small eye icon follows the text at reading pace, about 6 tokens a second, so it falls steadily behind the newest word. On 'Exactly the target', a white check-circle icon and the label 'the target' land beside the counter.

beats.say: It is not arbitrary. As a rule of thumb, it is roughly the slowest a model can go and still feel responsive.
beats.show: The 'slowed 4×' tag fades and the chat window dims to 40%, still streaming. On 'not arbitrary', a grey label writes under the counter: 'not arbitrary'. On 'rule of thumb', a white label lands beneath it: 'rule of thumb: slowest that still feels responsive'. The ruler keeps its 30 ms beat throughout; the counter's '33' glows once on 'responsive'.

beats.say: By the end, you will derive it from two numbers on a chip's specification sheet, for any model on any chip.
beats.show: The panel, ruler, chat window and labels fade to 20%. The stopwatch's '30 ms' lifts off, enlarges and settles centre top (960, 290) as a white stamp '≈ 30 ms per token', with a small grey line under it: 'the number this film is about'. On 'derive it', ch00's spec-sheet card slides up beneath it (x 700-1220, y 400-800): header 'chip spec sheet' and six grey placeholder lines. On 'two numbers', two of the lines brighten; on 'specification sheet', they resolve exactly as in ch00: amber 'operations per second: ?' and coral 'bytes per second: ?'. On 'any model on any chip', a fan of three faint chip icons and three model-file icons of different sizes riffles behind the card and settles. Hold.

scenes.name: one file, three homes
scenes.visual: One continuous shot: three capacity bars on one true scale, then the read speeds of the two that hold the whole file. Top band: the equation (centred, y 165) and, under it, the model as a solid coral block (x 200-1200, y 235-285). Three rows, all starting at x 200, each with an icon and a two-part title above its bar: disk (title y 350, bar y 375-425), memory beside the chip (title y 545, bar y 570-620), the chip itself (title y 740, bar y 765-815). Scale: 1,000 px = 140 GB. The memory bar is exactly 1,000 px. The disk bar runs off the right edge of the frame: truncated, not shrunk, so the scale still holds. The chip bar at this scale is 0.87 px, drawn as a 1 px hairline. Right zone (x 1260-1820) holds the magnifier and the two stopwatches. Colour: bars are blue outlines (containers), the model's bytes coral, the chip's working areas amber outlines, text white and grey. The takeaway band (y 952) is used in b5. The idea: one file, three homes of wildly different size and speed, and once the model is running only the middle one matters.

beats.say: At two bytes a weight, seventy billion weights make a hundred and forty billion bytes, a hundred and forty gigabytes.
beats.show: A file icon at (250, 165) opens into a small grid of coral weight tiles; on 'two bytes a weight', one tile enlarges with the tag '2 bytes'. The equation builds term by term at y 165: '70,000,000,000 weights' on 'seventy billion', '× 2 bytes', '= 140,000,000,000 bytes' on 'a hundred and forty billion bytes', which morphs into '= 140 GB' on 'gigabytes'; a grey note writes under its right end: '1 GB = 1 billion bytes'. The tile grid compresses into the solid coral block (x 200-1200, y 235-285) labelled '140 GB'.

beats.say: It lives in three places. A disk stores it. The memory beside the chip holds it while the model runs. The chip itself, which does the arithmetic, holds almost nothing.
beats.show: The equation dims to 40% and its grey note fades. On 'A disk', a hard-drive icon and the title 'A disk · stores the file' appear and the disk bar draws from x 200 rightward and off the frame edge; a 60% copy of the coral block slides into its left end; grey tag at the frame's right edge, above the bar: 'far more →'. On 'the memory beside the chip', a memory-module icon and the title 'Memory beside the chip · in use' appear and its bar draws to exactly 1,000 px; on 'while the model runs', the top coral block drops into it and fills it edge to edge. On 'The chip itself', a cpu icon and the title 'The chip itself · does the arithmetic' appear; on 'almost nothing', its bar draws as a 1 px hairline at x 200, with a grey tag beside it: 'to scale: under 1 px'.

beats.say: A few hundred thousand bytes in each small working area, a tenth of a gigabyte in all.
beats.show: The disk tag and the chip's 'to scale' tag dim to 30%. A magnifier circle, radius 120, swings from the hairline to (1500, 800), joined to it by a thin line, and enlarges it: inside, a grid of many small amber-outlined squares, the chip's working areas. On 'each small working area', one square highlights and a label lands left of the circle, right-aligned at x 1360, y 840: 'each: a few hundred thousand bytes'. On 'a tenth of a gigabyte', a second label lands above it at y 780: '≈ 0.1 GB in all · ≈ 1/1,000 of the model'.

beats.say: Reading it all off a fast disk takes about twenty seconds. From the memory beside the chip, tens of milliseconds.
beats.show: The magnifier and its labels dim to 30%; the three titles dim to 60%. Both reads run on one clock, time-compressed 10×; grey tag at (1500, 245): '10× time-compressed'. On 'off a fast disk', coral particles trickle out of the disk's block along a thin path down the left margin (x 170) into the chip's hairline, while a stopwatch above the disk bar at (1500, 300) counts up for two seconds of screen time to '≈ 20 s'; grey note right-aligned beside it at x 1450: 'fast drive ≈ 7 GB/s · varies'. On 'tens of milliseconds', the memory block fires one dense burst along its own short path into the hairline, over within a single frame (about 4 ms on the same 10× clock); its stopwatch at (1500, 595), right of the memory bar, snaps to 'tens of ms'. A white bracket joins the two stopwatches on their right (x 1790, y 300-595), with the label '≈ 500× faster' at (1620, 490), between the disk and memory rows.

beats.say: So the model is loaded once, at start-up, and stays put. The disk plays no part in making tokens. Everything happens in the middle tier.
beats.show: Stopwatches, bracket, notes and the 10× tag dim to 30%. On 'loaded once', a coral arrow draws from the disk's block down to the memory bar, labelled 'load once, at start-up', and the memory block flashes once. On 'stays put', a grey label writes under the memory bar at (200, 655): 'stays while the service runs'. On 'plays no part', the whole disk row fades to 20% and its tag swaps to 'start-up only, never per token'. On 'middle tier', the memory bar glows and the takeaway lands: 'the middle tier is where everything happens'.

scenes.name: paid once, spread thin
scenes.visual: One continuous shot along a single timeline: the life of the service, start-up at the left. The timeline runs across the centre (x 200-1720, y 520). At its left, a coral block 'load: many seconds' (schematic, 180 px wide at first); right of it an arrow, then a long blue band 'serve: a token every 30 ms' that fills with tiny blue tick marks, one per token. Top band: a token counter (centre, y 300) with a grey worked line under it (y 360). Lower third: a worked line (y 690) over a pair of bars drawn to one scale (y 770 and 830, both starting at x 460). Teal labels land above the timeline (y 440) in the last beat. The idea: a one-off cost shrinks to nothing when shared over millions of tokens; then a hint of a cost that every token pays again.

beats.say: Picture the model's working life: a load of many seconds, then a token every thirty milliseconds, for hours.
beats.show: On 'a load', the coral block 'load: many seconds' draws at the far left. On 'a token every thirty milliseconds', an arrow draws on and the blue band 'serve: a token every 30 ms' unrolls rightward to x 1720, filling with tiny ticks at a steady rhythm. On 'for hours', a grey label appears at the right end: 'hours →'.

beats.say: The load is real, but paid once. Shared among a day's millions of tokens, it is about seven millionths of a second each.
beats.show: On 'paid once', a small white tag '× 1' pins to the load block. On 'a day's', the timeline rescales to a full day: the right label becomes '24 hours', the ticks merge into a dense blue band, and the load block shrinks to its true width, a 0.35 px sliver, marked by a grey pointer 'load'. The top-band counter runs 0 to 2,880,000, label 'tokens', with the grey line under it 'one conversation, all day: 86,400 s ÷ 0.03 s'. On 'seven millionths', the lower third writes 'load share = 20 s ÷ 2,880,000 ≈ 7 millionths of a second'; beneath it, a blue bar 1,000 px long labelled '30 ms: the token itself' and, at the same left edge, a coral dot with a pointer 'load share', a quarter of a pixel at this scale; grey tag '≈ 0.02%'.

beats.say: A fixed cost stops mattering once spread over enough work. That is amortising. The rest of this film is about a cost that refuses to spread.
beats.show: The counter and the lower third dim to 30%. On 'a fixed cost', a teal label lands above the timeline: 'fixed cost ÷ lots of work → tiny'; on 'amortising', the word 'amortising' writes under it in teal. On 'refuses to spread', the teal labels dim and the camera pushes in on the timeline's right end: three consecutive ticks grow into blue token pills, each topped by its own coral block of the same size, with a '?' above the row and the label 'paid again, every token?'.

scenes.name: every token reads every weight
scenes.visual: One continuous shot. Centre-left: a GPU package seen from above (x 260-1240, y 330-830): the compute die in the middle, amber outline, label 'the chip · does the arithmetic'; two HBM stacks either side, blue containers full of coral weight tiles, label 'memory beside the chip · 140 GB'; joined to the die by a wide bus of parallel lines. Top band (y 165): the rule builds as an equation. Right column (x 1360-1820): first two counters, later the spec-sheet card from the opening scene. A label line under the package at y 880. The idea: the chip cannot keep the weights, so for one conversation every token drags all 140 GB across the bus, and the rule falls straight out of the picture.

beats.say: Here is that cost. Each token needs all seventy billion weights, which the chip cannot keep. So for one conversation, every token streams all hundred and forty gigabytes in from memory.
beats.show: The package fades in. On 'all seventy billion weights', the stacks fill with coral tiles. On 'cannot keep', a tiny region inside the die highlights with a grey tag '≈ 0.1 GB fits here'. On 'one conversation', a user icon with one blue pill appears just right of the die. On 'every token streams', coral particles flow along the bus in slices; as each slice arrives the die flashes amber for an instant and the slice fades. The counter 'bytes moved, this token' (1590, 400) runs 0 to 140 GB and a blue token pill pops out of the die; on 'from memory' it resets and runs again, faster, twice more, while 'tokens' (1590, 500) ticks 1, 2, 3. Label under the package: 'one conversation: all 140 GB, every token'; small grey tag at its right end: 'shared reads, many users: later'.

beats.say: Time per token is the bytes to read, divided by the bytes the memory delivers each second, its bandwidth. Hence the name, high bandwidth memory, H B M.
beats.show: The counters and the user icon fade out; the bus keeps flowing at a steady rate. The equation builds term by term on the spoken words: 'time per token' (white), '=', 'bytes to read' (coral), '÷' on 'divided by', 'bytes per second' (coral) on 'each second'. On 'bandwidth', a bracket draws under 'bytes per second' labelled 'bandwidth'. On 'high bandwidth memory', the stack label becomes 'HBM · high bandwidth memory'. The die label and the line under the package dim to 40%.

beats.say: Bandwidth is one of those two specification numbers. The other, how fast the chip calculates, does not even appear.
beats.show: The line under the package fades and, as the beat begins, the spec-sheet card from the opening scene slides into the right column (x 1380-1800, y 380-720) with its two lines, amber 'operations per second: ?' and coral 'bytes per second: ?'. On 'Bandwidth is one', the coral line brightens and a thin coral connector draws from it up to the equation's 'bytes per second'. On 'the other', the amber line pulses; on 'does not even appear', a white highlight sweeps the equation left to right and finds no amber term, and the amber line dims to 40% with a grey tag 'not in the rule'. A small amber tag settles beside the die: 'arithmetic ≈ 0.1 ms · overlaps the reading (later)'.

scenes.name: three chips, one division
scenes.visual: One continuous shot: one division done for three chips. Top band (y 165): 'time per token = 140 GB ÷ bandwidth', with 140 GB and bandwidth in coral. Directly below (y 255), a single centred worked-line band that holds one line at a time and is replaced row by row. A three-row table below it, rows centred at y 390, 530 and 670. Left column (x 120-500): chip cards, each a chip icon with name and bandwidth: 'H100 · 3.35 TB/s', 'H200 · 4.8 TB/s', 'B200 · 8 TB/s', with room for a small grey capacity tag under the name. Middle: coral bars from a common baseline at x 540, drawn to scale at 20 px per millisecond: 836, 583 and 350 px; each value sits at its bar's end. A dashed vertical line at 30 ms (x 1140, y 330-720), labelled '30 ms' at its foot. Grey tag under the table at (540, 760): 'bars to scale'. Right column (x 1620-1800): 'tokens / s', filled in the last two beats. Takeaway band (y 952) used in b5. The idea: thirty milliseconds is a division, and a figure that seems to clash with it is the same division on a different chip.

beats.say: The memory on Nvidia's H one hundred delivers three point three five terabytes a second, a terabyte being a thousand gigabytes. So each token takes forty-one point eight milliseconds.
beats.show: On 'Nvidia's H one hundred', the three cards slide in, H100 bright and the other two at 50%. On 'a terabyte being a thousand gigabytes', the worked-line band writes '3.35 TB/s = 3,350 GB/s', with a small grey '1 TB = 1,000 GB' beneath. On 'forty-one point eight', the band swaps to '140 GB ÷ 3,350 GB/s = 0.0418 s' and the H100 bar grows to 836 px with '41.8 ms' at its end. As the beat ends, a grey tag settles under the H100 name: 'holds 80 GB: a what-if'.

beats.say: The H two hundred takes twenty-nine point two. There are your thirty milliseconds, right on the target. The B two hundred, seventeen point five.
beats.show: On 'H two hundred', its card brightens; the band swaps to '140 GB ÷ 4,800 GB/s = 0.0292 s' and the bar grows to 583 px, '29.2 ms'. On 'thirty milliseconds', the row glows white and a stamp '≈ 30 ms' snaps onto the dashed line just past the bar's end; on 'the target', the white check-circle from the opening scene pops beside the stamp. A grey tag settles under the H200 name: 'holds 141 GB: a tight squeeze'. On 'B two hundred', its card brightens; the band swaps to '140 GB ÷ 8,000 GB/s = 0.0175 s' and the bar grows to 350 px, '17.5 ms'.

beats.say: Not a guess, not a benchmark: a division, the best the chip can do, and it moves with the model's size and the memory's speed.
beats.show: The worked line clears and the capacity tags dim to 30%. In the band, one phrase at a time, each replacing the last: 'not a guess', 'not a benchmark', then 'a division: the best case'. On 'the model's size', the '140 GB' in the equation pulses and briefly reads '70 GB' while all three bars shrink to half (418, 292, 175 px), hold, and spring back as '140 GB' returns. On 'memory's speed', the 'bandwidth' term pulses and the three bandwidth labels on the cards pulse top to bottom.

beats.say: Later you will meet about twenty-four tokens a second. A clash? One second divided by forty-one point eight milliseconds is twenty-three point nine, the H one hundred row.
beats.show: The band clears. Two blue quote cards land in it: left '30 ms → 33 tokens/s', right '≈ 24 tokens/s · later'; on 'A clash?', a '≠' between them flickers. On 'one second divided by', the right column gets its header 'tokens / s' with a grey '= 1 s ÷ time' under it, and the H100 cell fills '23.9' on 'twenty-three point nine'. On 'the H one hundred row', the '24' quote card slides down and docks beside the H100 cell.

beats.say: Same division, different chip. Running down clashes like that is a habit worth having.
beats.show: On 'Same division', the H200 cell fills '34.3' and the B200 cell '57.1'; the left quote card slides down and docks on the H200 row, its '33' beside '34.3' with a grey tag 'rounded from 30 ms'. The '≠' left in the band morphs into '=' and fades. On 'a habit', the takeaway lands: 'same division, different chips'.

scenes.name: everything between those two boxes
scenes.visual: One continuous shot, calm and spacious. Two large rounded blue boxes on one line, centred at y 520: left (x 180-760) 'A trained checkpoint' with sub-label 'weights on disk' and, inside it, a small drive icon holding the coral 140 GB block; right (x 1160-1740) 'A service that responds' with sub-label 'a token every 30 ms', a chat bubble inside streaming words at a true 30 ms beat, and a user icon just outside its right edge (x 1790). The gap between the boxes (x 760-1160) stays empty until the last word, when the white word 'inference' fills it. The idea: the whole subject of the film sits in the gap between a file and a responsive service.

beats.say: On the left, a trained checkpoint, the saved weights. On the right, a service that responds, a token every thirty milliseconds.
beats.show: The camera eases out from a close view of the empty centre to the full wide frame as the beat begins. On 'a trained checkpoint', the left box draws on, with its sub-label 'weights on disk' and the drive icon holding the coral block. On 'a service that responds', the right box draws on with 'a token every 30 ms'; its chat bubble starts streaming and the user icon fades in.

beats.say: Training made the checkpoint. Turning it into something a person can talk to, at a price that works, is a discipline of its own.
beats.show: On 'Training made the checkpoint', a faded grey tag 'training: done' appears above the left box. On 'Turning it into', a white arrow draws from the left box to the right box across the gap. On 'talk to', the user icon pulses; on 'a price that works', a small price-tag icon settles on the arrow.

beats.say: Why the reading, not the arithmetic, holds that gap at thirty milliseconds, not far less, is the rest of this film. Everything between those two boxes is inference.
beats.show: On 'the reading', coral particles start flowing along the arrow. On 'not the arithmetic', a faint amber ghost label '0.1 ms?' flickers beside the right box's '30 ms' and fades. On 'thirty milliseconds', '30 ms' glows. On 'inference', a soft white band fills the gap under the arrow and the word 'inference' writes on inside it, large. Hold for two seconds.

checks.claim: 70 billion weights × 2 bytes = 140,000,000,000 bytes = 140 GB
30 ms = 0.03 s, three hundredths of a second
one second of output at 30 ms per token ≈ 33 tokens

'at least as fast as you read': at a common estimate of 250 words a minute and ~1.5 tokens per word (ch01), reading is ≈ 6 tokens/s, ≈ 160 ms per token; 33 tokens/s is ≈ 5× that, so the eye icon in s01.b2 falls behind (estimate, not from the atlas)
s01 ruler: 1,400 px per second puts one pill every 42 px (30 ms); 33 pills in the second
disk: 140 GB at ≈ 7 GB/s (a fast NVMe drive; illustrative) ≈ 20 s, matching atlas fig 106's 'about 20,000 ms'

CORRECTION (reviewer): disk vs memory beside the chip = 20 s ÷ 41.8 ms ≈ 479× on an H100, shown as '≈ 500× faster' to match fig 106 and ch09 ('roughly five hundred times'); it rises to ≈ 686× (H200) and ≈ 1,143× (B200). The earlier draft's '500–1,000×' understated the top end
s02.b4 runs both reads on one 10×-compressed clock: disk 20 s → 2 s of screen time; H100 memory 41.8 ms → 4.2 ms, a single frame

CORRECTION to fig 12 'the chip holds a few hundred kilobytes': true per working area (an H100 SM has a 256 KB register file + 256 KB L1/shared), but the whole H100 holds 132 × 512 KB + 50 MB L2 ≈ 0.12 GB on chip. Film says both: 'a few hundred thousand bytes in each small working area, a tenth of a gigabyte in all' (same as ch09 and ch12)
140 GB is ≈ 1,150× the on-chip storage, so the chip holds '≈ 1/1,000 of the model'

CORRECTION to fig 12 'bars roughly to scale' (atlas draws the chip bar 60 px against the memory bar's 380 px): at true scale against a 1,000 px memory bar the chip bar is 0.87 px, so the film draws a 1 px hairline under a magnifier; the disk bar is truncated at the frame edge rather than shrunk
one conversation running all day at 30 ms per token ≈ 2,880,000 tokens ('a day's millions of tokens')
a 20 s load spread over 2.88 million tokens ≈ 0.0000069 s, 'about seven millionths of a second' per token
that load share is ≈ 0.02% of a 30 ms token
s03 bars: load share against a 1,000 px bar for 30 ms ≈ a quarter of a pixel; the 20 s load on a 1,520 px 24-hour timeline ≈ 0.35 px
H100 41.8 ms, H200 29.2 ms (the 'thirty milliseconds'), B200 17.5 ms per token
bars at 20 px per ms: 836 / 583 / 350 px; 30 ms marker at 600 px (x 1140 from the x 540 baseline)
s05.b3 what-if: a 70 GB model halves every bar to 418 / 292 / 175 px (20.9 / 14.6 / 8.75 ms)
tokens per second = 1 ÷ time per token: H100 23.9 ('about twenty-four', the later fig 130 figure), H200 34.3, B200 57.1
the rounded 30 ms gives 33.3 tokens/s, against 34.3 from the exact 29.2 ms; shown on screen ('rounded from 30 ms') rather than hidden
H100 holds 80 GB: the 140 GB model needs 1.75 H100s' worth of memory, overflowing one by 75%, so the H100 row is tagged 'a what-if'

CORRECTION (reviewer): H200 holds 141 GB (vendor spec). The film's round 140 GB leaves 1 GB spare, but the real Llama 3 70B (70,553,706,496 parameters, ch08/ch09) is 141.1 GB in 16-bit, which does not fit, and nothing else would fit beside it (ch13, fig 141). The draft's 'the model just fits' is replaced by the on-screen tag 'holds 141 GB: a tight squeeze'

Not adopted: the reviewer's line 'in practice spread over two chips, but the time per token comes from the same division'. Split over two H200s, each chip reads only 70 GB, so a token takes ≈ 14.6 ms, not 29.2. The line would imply the 29.2 ms still holds, so the capacity caveat stays on screen only
arithmetic per token ≈ 2 × 70e9 ops ÷ 989 TFLOP/s ≈ 0.14 ms, shown as '≈ 0.1 ms' to match the cold open; derived properly in ch05/ch10
